title: Fictional fixture: authority over a networked harbor signal system

period.label: 1950 network-control reorganization
period.note: The invented records bracket the dispute between a 1949 installation and a 1951 rule.

context.statement: Signal states can be changed remotely from a shared control network rather than by keepers at each entrance.

actors.label: Fictional Port Engineering Office
actors.role: Operates the network and requests discretion to alter signals during congestion.

actors.label: Fictional Municipal Harbor Council
actors.role: Claims authority to define the rules governing remote changes.

formulations.text: Who may authorize automatic or discretionary changes to shared harbor signals, and under what public rule?
formulations.reconstruction_note: No participant asks this exact umbrella question; it is reconstructed from conflicting requests about discretion and rule-making authority.

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A published condition under which the shared network may change a signal state.

institutions.label: Fictional Shared Signal Network
institutions.role: Makes remote and coordinated changes technically available.

stakes.statement: The dispute joins navigation safety to the legitimacy and auditability of remote decisions.

presuppositions.statement: A single network can observe and alter multiple signal states quickly enough for authority over changes to become a live issue.

accepted.statement: Permit automatic changes only under conditions published by the council.

marginal.statement: Allow the engineering office to override published conditions during congestion.

answer_space.scope_note: The fixture leaves the unthinkable category empty because the invented records do not support a boundary claim.

competing_formulations.text: How quickly may engineers clear congestion without waiting for a council vote?

sources.citation: Fictional Port Engineering Office, Shared Signal Network Installation Report (1949).
Fictional Municipal Harbor Council, Signal-Control Hearings (1950–1951).

evidence.excerpt: Installation began in 1949; the council shall review operating authority after two winters and issue a rule in 1951.
One desk may now observe and change every entrance signal without fuel delivery or attendance at the lamp site.
evidence.interpretation: Documents the altered technical and institutional conditions.

evidence.excerpt: During congestion the engineering desk must vary the signals at once, without awaiting a fresh council instruction.
evidence.interpretation: Supports the engineering formulation and discretionary answer.

evidence.excerpt: No shared signal shall change except under a condition stated beforehand in a public control rule.
The sessions repeatedly oppose immediate engineering discretion to prior public authorization.
evidence.interpretation: Summarizes the reconstructed problem without presenting it as a direct quotation.

evidence.excerpt: Options: council conditions only; engineering override with a written log; or an automatic schedule with no override.
evidence.interpretation: Bounds the documented governance answer space.

evidence.excerpt: This is the same harbor signaling question our predecessor board faced when it rationed lamp fuel.
evidence.interpretation: Records a later actor's continuity claim without deciding that the claim is correct.

identity_claims.note: Technical descent is documented, but the available material does not show whether actors inherited the earlier authority dispute or only its infrastructure.

continuity_evidence.note: The later data system is described as a descendant of the shared signal network.
Both episodes contain a demand that network decisions be governed by an accountable public rule.

discontinuity_evidence.note: Signal-state changes and retention of vessel histories are different immediate objects.
The later actors cite the inherited system but not the earlier control-authority debate.

target_object.note: The disputed operation changes from signal states to data retention.

stakes.note: Accountability overlaps, but privacy becomes a distinct later stake.

presuppositions.note: A shared infrastructure persists, while durable per-vessel histories are new.

answer_space.note: Control-rule options do not directly settle deletion and retention.

historical_recognition.note: Infrastructure lineage is explicit; problem lineage is not.

askability.note: Long-lived navigation histories create the later question's askability.

answer_transfer.reasoning: Rules for changing signals do not answer how long a vessel history may be retained.

presupposition_removal.reasoning: Shared control persists, but the later dispute depends on durable identity-linked records.

historical_recognition.reasoning: The system lineage is named while continuity of the debate remains unsupported.

relations.decision_note: The fixture deliberately retains undetermined as a high-confidence statement about evidential insufficiency, not as a weakly considered label.

hindsight_risks.description: A present-day analyst may call the episode an algorithmic-governance debate even though the actors use network-control language.
hindsight_risks.mitigation: Keep the reconstructed formulation tied to the two documented actor positions.

uncertainties.description: The umbrella formulation is not a sentence uttered by either side.
uncertainties.mitigation: Mark it actor_reconstructed, require two evidence items, and retain both competing formulations.
